extracted.intended_audience: employers, labor lawyers, HR professionals, gig platforms, worker advocates, and Department of Labor stakeholders assessing worker classification under the FLSA
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance and standards for applying the ‘control’ factor of the economic-reality test when distinguishing employees from independent contractors under the FLSA, with discussion of scheduling, supervision, pricing, reserved rights, and related indicia of control.

rubrics_metrics.name: Control factor (overall)
rubrics_metrics.description: Facts relevant to whether an employer controls economic aspects of the working relationship — the control factor of the economic reality/totality-of-the-circumstances test.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The Department frames the control factor from the employer's control over economic aspects of the relationship; scheduling, supervision, price-setting, reserved rights, and other indicia are facts to be weighed together. No single fact (e.g., scheduling flexibility) is dispositive; the totality of the circumstances determines whether a worker is economically dependent or in business for themself. The preamble and case law inform how each fact should be weighed; the regulatory text implements this at §795.105(b)(4).

rubrics_metrics.name: Scheduling flexibility / ability to set one's schedule
rubrics_metrics.description: Whether the worker can start and end work as they see fit or otherwise choose the timing/sequence/pace of work (i.e., scheduling flexibility).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Scheduling freedom may be probative of independent contractor status but, by itself, often provides only minimal evidence when other employer controls are present. Courts have found workers to be employees despite schedule flexibility. Employers may limit available hours, discipline or impose consequences for declining work, or otherwise constrain the practical ability to exercise flexibility; such constraints reduce the probative value of scheduling freedom. Scheduling flexibility should be evaluated alongside other forms of control and in context of industry/contract realities. The rule adopts the preamble's succinct statements for the regulatory text and relies on the preamble/subregulatory guidance for additional explanation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Supervision (including nontraditional forms)
rubrics_metrics.description: Whether the employer supervises the performance of the work, including reserve rights to supervise or discipline and supervision implemented through non‑in‑person means.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Close, in-person supervision is not required to find employee status; lack of direct supervision is not alone indicative of independent contractor status if other forms of control exist. Supervision may be exercised through training, hiring systems, job structure, or delegated/third‑party supervision reported back to the employer. The level of supervision necessary depends on the nature and skill required for the work. A totality-of-the-circumstances inquiry should consider both apparent and less-apparent forms of supervision.

rubrics_metrics.name: Technological supervision and algorithmic management vs mere monitoring/data collection
rubrics_metrics.description: Use of technological means (devices, electronic systems, algorithms) by an employer to supervise, direct, or correct a worker's performance — distinguished from mere data collection or monitoring for other business purposes.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Technological tools deployed to supervise the performance of work (including surveillance, productivity/location tracking, algorithmic management) can be probative of employer control and employee status. However, mere collection of data for unrelated business operations is not automatically supervision. The relevant question is whether technology is used to supervise/direct performance (including exercising reserved control when desired). The regulatory text references 'technological means of supervision (such as by means of a device or electronically)' and the preamble clarifies that monitoring only counts when it is used to supervise the work.

rubrics_metrics.name: Training and hiring systems as evidence of control
rubrics_metrics.description: Whether employers use pre-hire certification, initial training, or instructions that operate to control job performance even in the absence of day-to-day oversight.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Employers may rely on training and hiring systems to control performance such that lack of ongoing supervision does not indicate independence. Initial training or certification that effectively dictates how work is performed can be evidence of supervisory control; conversely, training that merely apprises workers of safety protocols or does not replace supervision is less probative. The preamble cites cases (e.g., Keller) where pre-hire systems supported a finding of control.

rubrics_metrics.name: Reserved rights to supervise or discipline (reserved control)
rubrics_metrics.description: Whether an employer retains the right to supervise, discipline, or otherwise control workers even if it does not regularly exercise that right.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: An employer’s reserved right to supervise or correct performance — including electing to exert control when it chooses — is relevant to the control analysis. Delegation of supervision to a third party does not eliminate the analysis: if the employer exercises or reserves supervisory control (even via delegation), that indicates control. The Department treats reserved control as a fact in the control factor (discussed elsewhere in the rule) and declines to add extensive regulatory text here, relying on preamble and future guidance for details.

rubrics_metrics.name: Ability to set or negotiate price/rate for goods or services
rubrics_metrics.description: Whether the worker sets or negotiates prices or rates for services (versus the employer controlling prices/rates).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Workers in business for themselves generally set or negotiate their prices; an employer’s command over price/rate tends to indicate the worker is not independent. Ability to negotiate and keep negotiated amounts (or to sell on the market) weighs in favor of independent contractor status. Conversely, accepting predetermined prices or lack of meaningful negotiation supports employee status. Presence of a contract setting prices does not automatically determine the outcome; the ability to negotiate or alter contractual terms is relevant.

rubrics_metrics.name: Contract terms and formal agreements are not dispositive
rubrics_metrics.description: The mere existence of a contract or written terms (e.g., a contract stating independent contractor status or setting prices) does not conclusively determine worker status.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A contract may reflect an allocation of expectations, but statutory/practical indicia of control remain the focus. Courts and the Department caution that contracts do not obviate a full economic‑reality analysis; examine whether the worker can meaningfully negotiate or change terms and the actual implementation of the contractual provisions.
